experiments.source: Codex on the requested Linux server, Python 3.12.3.
experiments.hypothesis: Consuming runs of non-quote characters reduces the regex work for SQL batches with long quoted vectors.
experiments.method: Three alternating process runs, same seeded 10000 rows of 128 dimensions, batches of 100, then 200 TopK queries. Compare complete query outputs. Also parse a fixed 100-row SQL batch 300 times with no storage work.
experiments.output: Write-phase seconds before [3.234867686, 2.938377720, 11.621469150], after [2.805967852, 2.690905519, 2.465986656]. Parse-only 1.3027 s before and 0.4636 s after. All three pairs returned identical 200 query results. 9841 short quote/space token inputs matched the prior pattern, escaped quotes parsed correctly, and 20 public cases plus two regression tests passed.
experiments.limits: Local timings include load on a shared server; write timings include data generation. No official score inferred.

experiments.source: Codex on the requested Linux server with Python 3.12.3
experiments.hypothesis: Tracking the logical append offset avoids a file-position lookup per log frame.
experiments.method: Three paired runs with 10000 rows, dimension 128, batches of 100, and 200 queries. Separately append 200000 buffered 64-byte payloads and verify every returned offset.
experiments.output: Write-phase seconds before [2.8393,2.8441,2.6745], after [2.4640,2.5567,2.6318]. All paired query results matched. Frame probe seconds before [0.2044,0.2072,0.2025], after [0.1310,0.1315,0.1296]. All 20 public cases and both regressions passed. After reopening a log with an uncommitted suffix, the next committed row reused the correct offset and survived another reopen.
experiments.limits: The frame probe excludes fsync. End-to-end local write timings include data generation. The alternative vector validation change was reverted after failing to improve the paired median.

experiments.source: Codex on the requested Linux server with existing Python 3.12.3
experiments.hypothesis: TopK already orders results by distance and primary key, so an equality index can group slots without sorting. Reusing an eligible cached column avoids rebuilds when AND predicates change order.
experiments.method: Three paired runs on 10000 rows. Cold path: perform 40 updates and time one filtered TopK after each. Mixed predicates: warm the g index and alternate g=0 AND h=0 and h=0 AND g=0 for 100 queries. Also compare 200 TopK results per pair in the existing 128-dimensional benchmark.
experiments.output: 20 groups, cold seconds before [0.4884,0.4861,0.4985], after [0.2984,0.2127,0.3044]. 10000 groups, cold seconds before [0.4953,0.3036,0.4916], after [0.4083,0.3817,0.3849]. Mixed predicates seconds before [1.1213,1.1208,0.7338], after [0.0497,0.0496,0.0496]. 128-dim query seconds before [1.7772,1.7785,1.7838], after [1.2282,1.3431,1.4682]. All compared results matched. All 20 public cases and two regression tests passed.
experiments.limits: Mixed-predicate workload deliberately stresses rebuild churn. The single-predicate warm test showed no consistent improvement. Timings are local and do not establish official score.

experiments.source: Codex on the requested Linux server with Python 3.12.3
experiments.hypothesis: When DELETE predicates use only the primary key, the live directory and pending transaction entries suffice to identify rows.
experiments.method: Three paired runs, each reopening 10000 rows of 128 dimensions to start with an empty row cache. Time 500 seeded random primary-key deletes in one transaction and a separate range delete of 1000 rows. Compare remaining primary keys with the expected set.
experiments.output: Point delete seconds before [0.0336,0.0270,0.0344], after [0.0190,0.0287,0.0252]. Range delete seconds before [0.1018,0.0752,0.1020], after [0.0121,0.0384,0.0415]. All remaining primary keys matched. All 20 public cases and 3 regression tests passed, including pending inserts and updates, contradictory predicates, rollback, and restart after an unfiltered delete.
experiments.limits: The range benchmark uses only the primary key. Mixed predicates still inspect row payloads. Point delete timings varied across runs.

experiments.source: Codex on the requested Linux server with existing Python 3.12.3
experiments.hypothesis: Queries projecting, filtering and ordering exclusively on the primary key can reuse the key directory path introduced for DELETE.
experiments.method: Three paired runs on 10000 rows of 128 dimensions. Reopen, time 500 random primary-key lookups, then 100 primary-key range queries with descending ORDER BY and LIMIT 10. Compare every response against expected keys.
experiments.output: Point query seconds before [0.01591,0.01988,0.02491], after [0.00753,0.01021,0.01304]. Range query seconds before [0.53812,0.48916,0.75986], after [0.22042,0.23374,0.36456]. Results matched. All 20 public cases and 3 regression tests passed. The regression covers aliases, duplicate key projections, LIMIT 0, pending inserts and updates, hidden deletes, and unchanged ordering without ORDER BY.
experiments.limits: This fast path applies only to primary-key-only queries. Timings are local and do not establish official scores.

experiments.source: Codex actual server experiment under /mnt/HDD2/zzp, system Python 3.12; no dependency changes

experiments.limitations: Local timing under variable shared server load, not an official score. Agent performed measurements; no claim of student-run experiments or guaranteed Agent Prompt marks.

experiments.source: Codex implementation and measurements on /mnt/HDD2/zzp/minivectordb-round2, system Python 3.12, no dependency changes
experiments.reasoning: Primary-key predicates and ordering can operate on the transaction-visible directory before fetching payloads. Scalar ordering does not need distances used only in output. Avoid per-row all(generator) for one predicate.
changes: Fetch only selected payloads for primary-key ordering/range queries
Use key directory to prefilter primary-key-only mutation candidates
Compute projection-only distances after scalar top-K selection
Specialize zero/one predicate loops
experiments.workload: 12000 rows, 128-dimensional vectors; 100 primary payload top-K, 100 primary-range distance projection, 60 scalar distance projection, 40 single-predicate filter, 15 full scan queries per run; three before/after pairs, order reversed in pair 2
experiments.correctness: All five workload result hashes equal across all six runs; 200 vector top-K query results byte-identical; 20 public cases and 7 regression tests pass. New tests cover transaction overlays, new tables, rollback, restart, aliases, multiple distances, extreme keys, and limited payload reads.

vector_smoke.note: Single paired smoke run, not a statistically established speedup; insert time varied from 2.629s to 2.905s although insert path unchanged.

experiments.limitations: Shared server timing, warm-cache scalar workload, not official score. Large scans exceeding cache and high-dimensional exact distance computation remain potential bottlenecks. These are agent-run experiments; no claim of student execution or guaranteed Agent Prompt points.

experiments.source: Codex implementation and measurements under /mnt/HDD2/zzp/minivectordb-round2, system Python; no environment dependency changes

external_reference.learning: PostgreSQL limits cache pollution caused by bulk scans. This implementation borrows that principle using admission control; it does not implement PostgreSQL ring buffers.

changes: Estimate a conservative cache weight lower bound from schema and committed row count
Only broad scans of tables exceeding the existing cache budget bypass eviction and LRU promotion; point queries, small tables, small result batches and small component groups use normal caching
Remove obsolete cached row versions after successful mutations; retain rollback cache clearing
Bind row reader once per scan to avoid repeated bound-method lookup
experiments.methodology: Three paired fresh-process runs per size (8000, 24000, 48000 rows, 128 dimensions), reverse order in pair 2; one warm-up, seven native timed exact top-10 queries, one separate untimed query counting decode misses. Median of per-process medians.
experiments.experiment_correction: The first benchmark wrapped every read to count misses during timing. Different keyword forwarding cost distorted small-table comparisons. Final evidence separates timing and counters; small-table overhead remains about 3 percent in final medians and is not concealed.
experiments.validation: 20 public protocol cases and 10 regression tests pass. All final benchmark result hashes match across revisions. Earlier mixed 200-query vector comparison also byte-identical before final reader-binding micro-optimization. Tests cover hot point rows, small-table warmup under full cache, memory accounting, updates/deletes, repeated pending versions, rollback and offset reuse.
experiments.limitations: Synthetic local warm-page-cache workload on a shared busy server; no official score or guaranteed Agent Prompt improvement. Conservative size estimate may miss large variable-length rows or pending inserts. Small-table median 12.390ms -> 12.750ms; 24000 rows 178.155ms -> 79.200ms; 48000 rows 242.073ms -> 222.779ms. This does not remove all bottlenecks.

experiments.source: DeepSeek implementation and measurements under /mnt/HDD2/zzp/minivectordb-round2, system /usr/bin/python3 3.12.3, numpy 2.3.5 unpacked from the cp312 manylinux wheel onto PYTHONPATH
experiments.problem: A new competition-shaped benchmark (10000 rows x 128 dims, 500 unfiltered + 500 filtered TopK, K=10) showed the unfiltered queries costing 15.9 ms each and 7.4 s of the 8.3 s query phase, while filtered queries cost 1.25 ms because the scalar equality groups already restrict candidates. math.dist over a 128-float list measures 1.22 us, and 10000 of those per query is essentially the whole cost, so the bottleneck was per-row Python distance computation, not decoding or the heap.
experiments.hypothesis: Materialise the live float32 vectors once into a dense matrix indexed by the existing stable index snapshot, compute every distance with a single BLAS mat-vec, and select Top-K with argpartition plus boundary tie expansion. The ranking key must stay (distance, primary key) and values must come from the stored float32 payloads, so exact semantics, the tie rule and float32 storage semantics are unchanged.

reference.learning: argpartition only guarantees that the k-th element is in place; elements equal to the boundary value may be split arbitrarily. That is why the implementation re-expands every candidate with distance <= boundary threshold before the final lexsort, instead of trusting the partition slice.
lexsort uses the last key as the primary key, so passing (primary_key, distance) yields distance-first ordering with primary-key tie-break, matching the SQL rule without a custom comparator.

einsum with an explicit float64 accumulator keeps the squared-distance sum in double precision even when the matrix is stored as float32, which keeps distances within the judge's 1e-5 tolerance of the previous math.dist results.

changes: Database.build_matrix: one pass over the index snapshot, assigning decoded float32 payloads and primary keys into dense arrays; float64 storage while it fits in 192 MiB, float32 beyond that
Database.matrix_top_k: single mat-vec for all distances, argpartition for the K-th threshold, boundary tie expansion, lexsort by (distance, primary key), then fetch only the K selected payloads
Table.matrix cache keyed to the snapshot object identity, invalidated together with blocks/axis/snapshot in Transaction.publish

Acceleration gated on: numpy importable, no WHERE filter, no pending transaction changes, exactly one distance ordering key ascending, LIMIT present, table >= 2048 rows and matrix bytes <= 192 MiB; otherwise the previous paths run unchanged
Dockerfile installs numpy==2.3.5 best-effort under a 300 s timeout and pins OPENBLAS/OMP/MKL to one thread; the pure-Python distance path remains the fallback
experiments.command: python3 tests/bench_competition.py <source> --tag <tag>;  OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 PYTHONPATH=/tmp/npydeps python3 tests/bench_competition.py <source> --tag cand
experiments.workload: 10000 rows x 128 dims, batches of 100 inserted through SQL, vector index created, 500 unfiltered + 500 filtered (category eq, 20 categories) TopK queries with K=10; three alternating rounds, medians reported
experiments.correctness: 20/20 public protocol cases pass in both modes (with and without numpy). 12 regression tests pass with numpy (the two new matrix tests execute) and 12 pass without numpy (2 skipped). The new tests compare the matrix path against a brute-force math.dist oracle after inserts, deletes, updates and inside a transaction, and assert exact/ann agreement plus LIMIT 0 and large tie groups. Selected ids for the full 1000-query benchmark are byte-identical to the baseline (ids_digest equal); distances differ only by summation order.
failed_attempts: First version used the delete bitmap directly as the live mask (flatnonzero(bits)). The new delete-after-build test caught it: every returned row was deleted. Fixed to flatnonzero(bits == 0).

The first oracle compared against the unrounded input doubles and failed by 1.2e-8. That was the test modelling storage wrongly, not an engine defect: rounding the fixture through struct float32 made the oracle exact.

Prefix / early-abandon pruning was considered and rejected before coding: for 128-dimensional data the partial squared distance crosses the K-th threshold only after most dimensions, so pruning saves little, and a Python-level early-exit loop is far slower than the C math.dist it would replace.
Default OpenBLAS threading measured 2.29 ms versus 1.94 ms with OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1, and unconstrained threading inside the judge container risks the 128-pid limit, so one thread was pinned.
experiments.regressions: Peak RSS grows by 35 MiB (numpy import about 30 MiB plus a 10 MiB matrix), which counts against the 20% memory component. The first unfiltered query also pays a one-off matrix build (about 140 ms at 10000 rows) that is inside measured time. Filtered queries are unchanged because the scalar group path already handles them.
unresolved: Whether the grading image really has numpy is unverified: neither the development machine nor the build server can run Docker, so the best-effort install plus fallback is the only guarantee. The fallback was measured at 7.9 s versus 8.3 s baseline for the same workload.
The matrix build re-decodes rows through read_row; reading packed frames directly into the matrix with frombuffer is an obvious follow-up that should cut the build cost.
The row cache still stores fully decoded vectors, so memory could drop substantially by keeping packed payloads and decoding lazily; that is the next candidate and was not attempted here.
Filtered TopK still needs a vector index for the scalar group path; without one it falls back to a full scan.
experiments.limitations: Shared-server timings with visible run-to-run variance (a single baseline workload varied 148-280 ms across the session), so only paired medians are quoted. These are DeepSeek executor experiments; the participant did not run or interpret them, and no Agent Prompt credit is claimed for them.

experiments.source: DeepSeek implementation and measurements under /mnt/HDD2/zzp/minivectordb-round2, /usr/bin/python3 3.12.3, numpy 2.3.5 unpacked onto PYTHONPATH, OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1
experiments.baseline: 274d62f (previous candidate in this session); original scoring baseline 716867c0103984aa840f6d4de07d69b8d31746c0
experiments.problem: After the dense matrix landed, unfiltered TopK still cost 2.32 ms and filtered TopK 1.23 ms. An isolated kernel probe showed the direct kernel at 1.514 ms for 10k x 128, of which 1.198 ms was just allocating the 9.8 MiB (values - query) temporary, while a BLAS mat-vec took 0.317 ms and the selection step 0.030 ms. Filtered queries still ran math.dist per candidate row.
experiments.measurement: scripts/probe_kernels.py: direct 1.514 ms (subtract 1.198 ms, select 0.030 ms), float64 matvec 0.317 ms, float32 matvec 0.160 ms; max |identity - direct| = 3.55e-15 on the benchmark data.
experiments.hypothesis: Computing |v-q|^2 as |v|^2 - 2 v.q + |q|^2 replaces the element-wise pass with one BLAS mat-vec and removes the matrix-sized allocation; with per-row norms precomputed and a coordinate-magnitude guard, the cancellation error stays far below the judge tolerance. For filtered queries the equality groups already identify the candidate slots, so distances only need to be computed for those slots rather than for every scanned row.

reference.learning: d^2 = |a|^2 + |b|^2 - 2 a.b is the law of cosines; the subtraction cancels when the vectors are close relative to their length, which is exactly why the identity is only used while coordinates stay below the 1000 guard and the direct kernel handles the rest.
matmul dispatches to BLAS for 2-D by 1-D, so one call computes all row dot products; the repeated temp allocation, not the arithmetic, was the real cost.

changes: build_matrix stores per-row squared norms and the maximum absolute coordinate alongside values and keys
matrix_top_k uses the identity kernel below the magnitude guard, works on squared distances for selection and tie expansion, and takes only K square roots for the output
ensure_groups extracted from component_offsets so equality groups can be built independently of whether a vector index exists
matrix_group_top_k maps an equality group's slots straight into the matrix, computing distances only for those rows and returning None so the generic path still handles oversized groups
experiments.command: python3 scripts/probe_kernels.py; python3 tests/bench_competition.py <src> --tag t; OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 PYTHONPATH=/tmp/npydeps python3 tests/bench_competition.py <src> --no-index --tag t
experiments.workload: 10000 rows x 128 dims, batches of 100, 500 unfiltered + 500 filtered TopK (K=10), with and without CREATE VECTOR INDEX; three alternating rounds, medians reported
experiments.correctness: 20/20 public protocol cases pass with and without numpy. 14 regression tests pass with numpy (4 skipped without). New tests cover the magnitude guard at the float32 boundary (16777216 and 16777217 must both yield exact zero distance), filtered group selection including an empty group and LIMIT 0, and deletes after the group and matrix are built. Selected ids for the full 1000-query benchmark are byte-identical to the baseline in both the indexed and the no-index scenario.

differential_fuzz.method: 3000-row table with duplicated vectors (distance ties), negative keys, four equality groups; 120 generated queries per seed covering exact/ann, eq/neq filters, LIMIT 0/1/3/10/50/400, ORDER BY id DESC, SELECT *, multiple distance projections; run against the baseline and the candidate source with the same seed, then compare ids exactly and distances to 1e-9

failed_attempts: The first large-coordinate test expected ids [0,2,4,6,8] for LIMIT 5 on a table where 1500 rows tied at distance 0. The engine was right and the expectation was wrong: ties are broken by primary key, so LIMIT 5 returns the five smallest keys. The fixture was rebuilt with only five rows at distance 0 so the boundary behaviour is what the test actually pins down.
Keeping squared distances for output was considered and rejected: the judge compares distances, so the K selected rows still take a square root; only the 10k-row sqrt was removed.

Sorting by squared distance was initially suspected to change tie behaviour; verified that squaring is monotone on non-negative values, so equal distances stay equal and the primary-key tie-break is unaffected.
experiments.regressions: Peak RSS stays at 114 MiB (unchanged from the previous step). Building equality groups costs one full row pass on the first filtered query (inside measured time) and is discarded on any mutation, so alternating write/filter workloads can rebuild it repeatedly; that pre-existing behaviour was not changed.
unresolved: Non-equality scalar filters (>, <, BETWEEN-like ranges) still require a full row scan; only equality groups feed the matrix.
Multiple AND predicates use only the single-term accelerated path and otherwise fall back.
The matrix is invalidated on any committed mutation, so a write-heavy interleaving rebuilds it; no incremental update was attempted.

MAX_BLOCK_ROWS (50000) disables equality groups for larger tables; a 100k-row filtered query then falls back to a full scan at 474 ms in both the baseline and the candidate, so this is a pre-existing limit rather than a regression. Large-table unfiltered TopK still improved from 576 ms to 11.5 ms.
numpy availability in the grading image is still unverified end to end because no Docker runtime is available on either machine.
experiments.limitations: Shared-server paired timings only; the baseline column also moved between rounds (15.3-16.4 ms), which is why ratios rather than absolutes are emphasised. DeepSeek executor experiments; no participant-run measurement and no Agent Prompt credit claimed.

experiments.problem: The 10k-row write phase takes about 1.4 s (100 committed batches of 100 rows). Before changing anything, measure where the per-batch cost goes and decide whether a safe optimisation exists.
experiments.hypothesis: If SQL parsing dominated, a parser fast path would be the win; if fsync dominated, nothing safe can be done because commit durability is a hard requirement.
experiments.conclusion: Per 100-row batch: parse 0.95 ms, typed() validation of 100 vectors about 3 ms, log write plus fsync 2.96 ms (of which 1.99 ms is write+fsync alone on this filesystem). No single component dominates, and the two largest are (a) mandatory durability and (b) required float32 validation that the spec demands. Micro-optimising validation to use map(math.isfinite, ...) and dropping the redundant type check might save 0.1-0.15 s of the 1.4 s, which is below the run-to-run noise on this shared host, so no code change was made.
experiments.limitations: Single measurement host with shared I/O; fsync cost depends on the storage device and the judge machine may differ substantially. This entry records a rejected optimisation, not a verified improvement.

experiments.source: DeepSeek implementation and measurements under /mnt/HDD2/zzp/minivectordb-round2, /usr/bin/python3 3.12.3, numpy 2.3.5, OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1
experiments.problem: After the matrix and equality-group work, peak RSS rose from 80 MiB (baseline) to 114 MiB because the bulk build that fills the matrix also inserted every decoded row into the 96 MiB LRU row cache, storing the same vectors twice. Memory is 20% of the scoring formula, so this was a scored regression.
experiments.hypothesis: The matrix and the equality groups are self-contained representations; the build pass does not need the LRU cache. Adding a cache=False mode to read_row for bulk builds should remove the duplicate storage without changing query cost, because only the K projected rows per query need caching.
changes: read_row(table, offset, scan=False, cache=True) with cache=False skipping admission and eviction
build_matrix and ensure_groups read with cache=False
projection reads in matrix_top_k / matrix_group_top_k keep the default cache=True so result rows stay hot
experiments.command: python3 tests/bench_competition.py <src> --tag t; paired 3-round script over baseline and candidate
experiments.correctness: 14 regression tests pass with and without numpy; 20/20 public cases unchanged; the full 1000-query ids_digest is unchanged from the previous candidate (38e0d153...), so selection semantics are untouched.
experiments.regressions: Projection rows are now read from the log instead of a pre-warmed cache on the first query after a build; the effect is inside the noise floor here (10 rows per query). Repeated queries on tables small enough to skip the matrix still use the normal cache path, so nothing regressed there.
failed_attempts: Making every read uncached was rejected: small tables rely on the LRU cache for repeated point queries, so cache=False is limited to the two bulk builders.
Dropping the vector payload from cached rows (lazy decode) was considered as a follow-up but not attempted in this step; it would need consistent handling in UPDATE re-encoding and vector projection.
experiments.limitations: Local shared-server measurement; peak RSS is process RSS, not the cgroup memory.peak the judge uses, so the absolute number is indicative only. DeepSeek executor experiment; no participant-run measurement claimed.

experiments.problem: Transactional and recovery semantics are the highest-risk part of the submission: one wrong assertion in a formal case sets the whole score to zero, yet the existing tests only covered a handful of fixed scenarios. Separately, UPDATE returned the number of matched rows rather than the number of rows whose value actually changed.
experiments.hypothesis: A model-based random test (Python dict of committed rows plus a transaction overlay) can predict visibility for every operation, including after restarts, and will expose any divergence between the engine and MySQL-like semantics before the judge does.
changes: tests/test_model_fuzz.py: 220 random operations over a 240-row table - multi-row INSERT, predicate UPDATE on g/s/v, predicate DELETE, BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK, repeated process restarts, and TopK queries compared with brute force; every statement's affected_rows is predicted by the model
UPDATE counts only rows whose stored value actually changes (MySQL semantics); vector columns are compared in their packed float32 form so the comparison is exact
README rewritten as a reference document for the current design (build/run, SQL scope, error codes, end-to-end example, row-log format, the four query paths, limitations)
experiments.command: cd tests && PYTHONPATH=<src> python3 -m unittest test_model_fuzz -v; python3 protocol_check/run.py --command '[...]' --output <dir>
findings: The harness itself was wrong first: SQL literals formatted with %.6g lose float32 digits (4.05e-6 error at the restart comparison). Switching the generator to repr() made the round-trip exact.
The engine reported 19 affected rows for UPDATE t SET s='c' WHERE g=0 while only 12 rows changed value, because unchanged rows were re-written. Fixed to skip unchanged rows.
experiments.correctness: 15 regression tests pass with numpy and 15 without (4 skipped); 20/20 public protocol cases pass in both modes; the model fuzz runs 220 operations with inserts, updates, deletes, commits, rollbacks, restarts and 20+ TopK comparisons and matches the model exactly.
experiments.regressions: None measured: affected_rows only shrinks for no-op updates, and the benchmark write/query timings are unchanged because inserts do not go through UPDATE.
experiments.risks: Counting changed rows is a judgement call. If the formal reference counts matched rows, a no-op UPDATE case would expect the larger number. It was chosen because the task is described as a MySQL case suite and MySQL's affected_rows counts changed rows; the previous behaviour (matched rows) was the alternative.
experiments.limitations: The fuzz runs at small scale (240 rows, 3 dimensions) so it exercises semantics rather than performance; the matrix fast path is only reached by the dedicated matrix tests. DeepSeek executor experiment; no participant-run measurement claimed.

limitations: The bitmap proposal and constraints are participant statements. Code analysis, experiments and explanations are Agent work. No participant-run experiment or independent interpretation is claimed. The dense-matrix-topk experiment was executed by DeepSeek on the participant's server under the participant's stated boundary constraints (no fsync/commit/rollback changes, no exact-result or float32 or tie-order changes); the participant supplied the direction list and constraints but did not run or interpret the measurements.

learning_cases.agent_investigation: Inspecting the old row log corrected the initial premise: DELETE already appended a tombstone. The avoidable cost was discarding both in-memory indexes and rebuilding them on the next query. The implementation retains stable snapshot slots and applies the invalidation bit only after durable commit.

verification.source: Codex on the requested Linux server using existing Python 3.12.3.
verification.method: Insert 10000 rows (id=i, g=i%10, vector=[i,0]), warm the filtered scalar blocks and unfiltered vector axis, DELETE WHERE id=0, reset the read_row call counter, then query both TopK paths with target [0,0], K=2. Filtered query uses WHERE g=0.
verification.output: Before bitmap: 20999 read_row calls. With bitmap: 1001 read_row calls. Correct IDs in both versions: unfiltered [1,2], filtered [10,20].
verification.scope: Counts row accessor calls, including cache hits. Does not measure disk reads.

learning_cases.agent_interpretation: The bitmap keeps the prior snapshot usable for delete-heavy interleaving. One billion bits require 125000000 bytes (~119.2 MiB), excluding row and offset metadata. A snapshot is retired once at least half its slots are dead; the tests verify this transition but do not establish an optimal threshold.
